description: Trigger evals for post-review-pivot: it fires when a review changes the intended approach and the task needs a keep versus replace digest, while pr-feedback-ingest, implement-slice-complement, sync-task-state, task-init and direction-adjust handle corrective comments, trivial fixes, memory drift, unrelated new work, and self-found course corrections.

should_trigger: the reviewers said we picked the wrong integration shape, so what do we keep and what do we throw away?

PR #148 came back with a big one from the tech lead: we should store the totals on the invoice row, not compute them from line items in a view. Two migrations and the serializer are now wrong. Sort out what survives and what has to be redone.
Team review decided the export should be a scheduled job instead of an on-demand endpoint. Slices 02 and 03 assumed the endpoint. Write up the pivot and the smallest set of plan updates, no code yet.

After the design review the field we built everything around, customer_ref, turns out to be the wrong identifier. Capture the change in direction, mark which slices stay valid, and tell me what to rewrite.
review says the whole caching layer should go through the gateway instead of the service. I need a digest of what is now revert or replace before I touch the plan.

should_not_trigger.prompt: Greptile left 9 comments on PR #148: a missing null check, two naming nits and a stale test. Map each one to files and slices so I can fix them under the current plan.
A reviewer spotted a typo in an error message and a missing log line inside the approved slice. Just apply the fix.
The review is done and nothing changed in direction, but TASK_STATE.md still says slice 02 is in progress. Bring the state file up to date.
A teammate commented that we should also build a notification center. That is a different feature altogether, so open it as its own task.
Nobody has reviewed anything yet, but I feel like the approach we chose might be wrong. Record this course correction from my own work in the decisions file.
